posts.name: Ganesh Eswar
posts.cooked:
Sir, we have come up lot of editors so which one we all should familar with?
@PUNEET @chaitanya353535

posts.name: User
posts.cooked:
That’s a great question!

1. ed (1969) – The Original Unix Editor

  • History: Created by Ken Thompson in 1969 for Unix.
  • Importance:
    • First text editor on Unix.
    • Line-oriented, minimalistic, and efficient for slow terminals.
    • Foundation for later editors like ex and vi.
    • Still available on modern Unix/Linux systems.

2. ex (1976) – Extended ed

  • History: Created by Bill Joy at UC Berkeley in 1976 as an improvement over ed.
  • Importance:
    • Introduced a visual mode (vi), making editing more interactive.
    • Added features like command-line substitution (s/search/replace/g).
    • Still available on Unix/Linux as a legacy editor.

3. vi (1978) – The Classic Visual Editor

  • History: Developed by Bill Joy in 1978 as an improvement over ex.
  • Importance:
    • Became the default Unix editor.
    • Mode-based editing: command, insert, and visual modes.
    • Fast and efficient for large files and slow networks.
    • Led to more advanced versions like vim (Vi IMproved).

4. emacs (1976-1985) – The Extensible Editor

  • History:
    • First developed in 1976 by Richard Stallman and Guy Steele.
    • GNU Emacs (1985) became the most popular version.
  • Importance:
    • Highly customizable and extensible with Lisp.
    • Supports advanced features like version control, mail, and even games.
    • Competes with vi in the long-standing “vi vs. emacs” debate.

5. nano (1999) – The Beginner-Friendly Editor

  • History:
    • Developed in 1999 as a free replacement for pico (which was tied to Pine email).
  • Importance:
    • Simple, easy-to-use interface with on-screen help.
    • No modes like vi, making it beginner-friendly.
    • Default editor for many Linux distributions.

Which One to Learn?

  • Beginners: nano (easy to use).
  • System Admins: vi or vim (available everywhere and I use this one).
  • Programmers: vim or emacs (powerful, extensible).
  • Unix Purists: ed or ex (if you want historical knowledge).

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked: Also people who are interested to extend vim further with extensions and want LSP support and in general a IDE feel from vim, I would recommend looking into neovim or nvim in short. There are some pre-configured rices of nvim, such as nv-chad and astrovim.
